extracted.intended_audience: researchers and staff involved in grant peer review (panel chairs, reviewers, scientific review officers, and funding agency personnel)
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluation of the quality, effectiveness, and influence of grant peer review panel discussions — i.e., how panels conduct discussion, how discussion is facilitated, and how discussion affects scoring and funding decisions. Useful for designing/improving panel procedures and chair training.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer participation
rubrics_metrics.description: Level of active involvement by reviewers in panel discussion, including both assigned and unassigned reviewers (paper notes 92% felt reviewer participation occurred).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure whether discussion is driven only by assigned reviewers or includes input from unassigned reviewers. Examples/anti-patterns: 'Discussion was driven by the assigned reviewers. Sometimes an interested non-assigned reviewer would get involved.'; 'Non-assigned reviewers rarely ask questions.' Consider frequency of comments from unassigned reviewers as an indicator.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarification of differing opinions
rubrics_metrics.description: Extent to which discussion helps clarify and resolve differing opinions among reviewers (Q2: 70% found discussions useful/very useful for clarifying opinions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good discussions expose why reviewers disagree and produce clearer rationales for scores. Example positive comment: 'Bringing those things out in discussion helps assure more fairness of scores.' Anti-pattern: panels that accept the primary reviewer at face value and do not probe dissenting views.

rubrics_metrics.name: Informing unassigned reviewers / sufficiency of format and duration
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the discussion format and duration allow non-assigned reviewers to be well-informed enough to cast merit scores (Q3: 79% agreed discussions were sufficient).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether unassigned reviewers have read proposals or rely solely on discussion; short times and lack of prep can result in superficial or biased scoring. Quotes: 'There really is not enough time for non-assigned reviewers to be able to read the grants and listen to the discussion.' Consider asking unassigned reviewers to read abstracts/critiques ahead of time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discussion quality (openness, balance, lack of bias, focus, efficiency)
rubrics_metrics.description: Overall quality of discourse defined by openness, balance, absence of bias, focused content on key points, and efficiency (paper's operational definition of discussion quality).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good quality = openness and balance, focused debate on key issues, minimal biased language. Metrics: proportion reporting 'fair and balanced' (88%). Anti-patterns: 'herd mentality', uneven focus, overly polite panels that avoid frank criticism, or discussions dominated by rhetoric rather than rationale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chair facilitation (leadership and moderation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Effectiveness of the chair in directing, limiting, policing, encouraging participation, focusing debate, and mitigating bias (Q4: 68% found chair involvement extremely/very useful).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chair responsibilities include moderating personalities, limiting inappropriate or prolonged remarks, encouraging differing opinions, and directing discussion to key points. Examples: 'A good chair is absolutely essential' vs 'Most have done a poor job, even to the point of not cutting off inappropriate questions.' Training and selection of chairs are recommended if chairs are ineffective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Influence of discussion on outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Degree to which panel discussion changes preliminary scores or affects final funding decisions (Q5: 71% agreed discussion influenced outcomes, but magnitude of change is often small).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess percent of proposals with pre- to post-discussion funding-line shifts and magnitude of score changes. Note caveats: many discussions produce small shifts; discussions may more often point out weaknesses (negative shifts) than elevate proposals. Anti-pattern: discussion rarely changes outcomes or only serves to ratify initial assessments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promotion of the best science and support for innovation
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether discussions help select and promote the best and most innovative science (Q6: 60% agreed discussions promoted the best science), and whether panels are overly conservative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Watch for conservatism and risk-aversion that disadvantage innovative (high-risk/high-reward) proposals: 'Truly innovative grants ... Panels often go for ‘safe’ bets.' Consider whether discussion norms or scoring discourage innovation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of whole panel expertise / cross-expertise dialogue
rubrics_metrics.description: Extent to which panels leverage varied expertise across members and create dialogues between reviewers of different expertise areas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good panels promote cross-expertise exchange so unassigned reviewers benefit from specialist perspectives. Anti-pattern: limited dialogue across expertise areas, opportunities for cross-talk are rare, reducing the advantage of convening a panel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discussion time management and sufficiency
rubrics_metrics.description: Adequacy of allotted time and time use during discussions; includes presenters focusing on key points and chairs limiting overlong presentations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Short discussion times can exacerbate bias and prevent meaningful exchange: 'Some reviewers spend too much time presenting their review, ... leaving less opportunity for discussion.' Chairs should enforce limits and keep focus on key aspects to ensure fairness and thoroughness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uneven influence / dominance by individual reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: Risk that certain reviewers (e.g., primary reviewers, assertive personalities, or subject-matter 'strong' reviewers) disproportionately influence scores and outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indicators: deference to primary reviewer, assertive reviewers swaying quieter ones, or a single reviewer 'making or breaking' borderline grants. Mitigation: chair intervention, balanced discussion, and accountability for claims. Example: 'The stronger reviewer will prevail.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Score calibration talk and accountability
rubrics_metrics.description: Instances where panelists explicitly reference others' scoring habits or hold them accountable (e.g., 'your comments are meaner than your score') and the role such talk plays in aligning scores.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Score-calibration talk is correlated with scoring shifts; encourage accountable, descriptor-based calibration to align critiques and scores. Chairs may facilitate calibration talk to improve consistency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communication channel quality (face-to-face vs teleconference)
rubrics_metrics.description: Impact of meeting modality on discussion richness and influence; face-to-face communication is a richer channel than virtual alternatives and tends to yield larger scoring shifts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect shorter discussions and smaller post-discussion score changes in teleconference panels. Consider channel effects when designing review processes and scheduling time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sources of bias related to discussion
rubrics_metrics.description: Various biases introduced or amplified by discussion processes, including individual reviewer bias, unassigned reviewer reliance on discussion rather than reading, group-think, and conservatism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify and mitigate bias sources through chair moderation, promoting diverse viewpoints, encouraging evidence-based argumentation, and possibly using impartial observers. Examples: 'it takes just one panel member to cast doubt on a grant.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Chair training and application of leadership/team-communication science
rubrics_metrics.description: Need for formal chair training and review procedures informed by leadership and team communication research to improve facilitation and reduce bias.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paper recommends improving chair training in management of discussion and implementing procedures informed by the science of leadership and team communication to enhance consistency, inclusivity, and impartiality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Panel composition and number/assignment of reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: Design choices about how many reviewers are assigned per proposal and how assignments are made (affects bias, workload, and leveraging panel expertise).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider optimizing number of assigned reviewers and alternative practices (e.g., asking unassigned reviewers to read abstracts/critiques) to reduce reliance on discussion-only information and mitigate bias from too few assigned readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fairness and balance in scoring process
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the process and discussion produce fair and balanced treatment of proposals, including mitigation of extremes and equitable consideration of all viewpoints (paper reports 88% felt discussions were fair/balanced).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether chairs adjust for extremes (overly laudatory or extremely negative reviews) and whether quieter reviewers' logical reasons are heard rather than being overridden by assertiveness. Anti-pattern: scores based on assertiveness rather than logic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encouraging dissent and frank opinions
rubrics_metrics.description: Degree to which panel culture and chair behaviour encourage frank critique and dissent rather than politeness that suppresses negative but necessary evaluations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Positive practices: chairs actively solicit dissenting views; create norms where frank, evidence-based criticism is acceptable. Anti-pattern: 'On the whole, I felt most panel members were too polite and unwilling to offer frank opinions of weak proposals.'
